feedback: If a learner thinks adding alkali just 'waters down' the acid, highlight that the pH moves through 7 into the alkaline range — adding water alone would only bring an acid's pH closer to 7, never past it, so the acid and alkali must be reacting and cancelling.
If a learner stops reasoning at neutral, have them add more alkali and observe the swing into the alkaline (blue/purple) range, showing 7 is a point you can pass.
If a learner predicts the colour will stay the same, pause and have them compare prediction with the observed shift.
activities.intendedInsight: Mixing an acid with an alkali moves the pH toward 7 — they react and cancel rather than simply coexist. For a strong acid and strong alkali, neutral (7) is a precise crossing point; adding more alkali beyond it turns the solution alkaline, showing that neutral is a point on the scale you can pass, not an end point where nothing more can change.
learnerActions: Start with a strongly acidic solution that reads red (low pH) on indicator and meter.
Add alkali in small steps (drop by drop near neutral, where the pH changes very quickly) and watch the pH climb and the indicator colour change through orange and yellow to green around neutral (7).
Keep adding alkali past neutral and observe the colour continue into blue then purple as the solution becomes alkaline.
Describe in your own words what neutralisation means: an acid and an alkali cancel toward pH 7.
Predict, before each addition, which way the pH and colour will move; check against what you observe.
activities.title: Neutralisation mixer: watch pH move toward 7

feedback: If a learner says 'more concentrated means stronger and more dangerous', separate the two ideas explicitly: strength = degree of H+ release (fixed for the acid); concentration = amount dissolved (adjustable by dilution). Compare citric (weak) and hydrochloric (strong) at matched concentrations.
If a learner assumes all acids burn, point to weak acids in food — citric in fruit, acetic in vinegar, carbonic in fizzy drinks — and note corrosiveness depends on strength AND concentration.
If a learner describes neutral as 'nothing in it', explain neutral means acidic and alkaline effects balance (equal H+ and OH-), as in pure water, not emptiness.
If a learner says diluting a strong acid makes it 'a weak acid', clarify it becomes a dilute strong acid — strength is unchanged, only concentration drops.

After observing the matched-concentration test, confirm that the strong acid (hydrochloric) reads the lower pH; full-mark reasoning cleanly separates 'how much acid' (concentration) from 'how readily it gives H+ ions' (strength).
activities.intendedInsight: Strength and concentration are different: strength is how fully an acid releases H+ ions (a property of the acid — hydrochloric is strong, citric is weak), while concentration is how much acid is dissolved and can be changed by dilution. At matched concentration the strong acid reads the lower pH; more broadly, corrosiveness depends on both strength and concentration, so a concentrated weak acid is not automatically more dangerous than a dilute strong one. Weak acids like citric and acetic are safe to eat at the low concentrations found in food, although concentrated forms can still be corrosive.
learnerActions: Consider two bottles: very concentrated citric acid (the acid in lemons) and dilute hydrochloric acid.

Predict and explain your reasoning BEFORE testing, focusing on the difference between strength and concentration — note that which bottle is more corrosive (or reads lower pH) depends on the actual concentrations and cannot be settled by 'more concentrated' alone.

To get a determinate comparison, test equal-concentration solutions of citric and hydrochloric acid with universal indicator or a pH probe, and predict which reads the lower pH and why, before testing.
Observe the readings and compare them to your prediction.
Explain the result by separating how MUCH acid is dissolved (concentration) from how readily the acid releases hydrogen ions, H+ (strength).
activities.title: Strength vs concentration: predict, observe, explain
